editorial:
The Adventures of Robin Hood (premiered August 18, 1922) was the most expensive American film produced to that date, with Douglas Fairbanks's own production company spending approximately $1.4 millionâ€”a substantial portion of it on an 80-acre castle set on the United Artists lot in Hollywood, then the largest standing set in film history. Director Allan Dwan built the film around Fairbanks's signature acrobatic physicality: the Earl of Huntingdon leaps from parapets, vaults up curtains, and slides down drawbridge chains in sequences that defined the swashbuckler genre for a generation. At roughly 170 minutes it is one of the longest American silent films ever made, and its scaleâ€”tournament pageants, pitched siege warfare, elaborate banquet halls packed with hundreds of extrasâ€”makes it a uniquely rich source of medieval visual material unavailable at this production quality anywhere else in the public domain.

The rights position is clean on the print and completely tangled on the audio. The 1922 US publication date clears the pre-1930 bright line without any need to check renewal records: this film is public domain in the United States, period. The practical trap is that every commercial copy in wide circulationâ€”including Kino Lorber's DVDâ€”arrives bundled with a newly composed or arranged musical score whose composer retains independent copyright in that recording. Using footage ripped from a commercial disc without stripping the audio infringes that score even though the images are free. The verified-safe path is the silent or openly licensed print on the Internet Archive; read the item-page license statement on the score before any commercial release.
faq: Can I use footage from a Kino Lorber DVD of this film?

The visual content of the 1922 film is public domain, so the images themselves are free. The Kino Lorber release bundles a separately composed musical score and sound recording that are independently copyrighted. You may use the video trackâ€”muted or with your own audioâ€”without infringing. Using the disc's audio track in a commercial release requires clearance from the score's rightsholder.
This film has nearly the same title as the 1938 Errol Flynn pictureâ€”are they connected for rights purposes?

They are legally distinct works with no shared rights. The 1938 Warner Bros. The Adventures of Robin Hood is a separate copyrighted film and is not in the public domain. Only the 1922 Fairbanks film is free to use. Verify your source material carefully before publishing, since the near-identical titles cause frequent mislabeling on streaming platforms and download sites.
